blocks.text: Verse 20. And I will remove the northern one far from you, and drive him into a thirsty and desolate land: his face toward the eastern sea, and his rear toward the hinder sea. And his stench shall go up, his foulness, I say, shall go up; because he has done great things.] Those who refer these things to the Chaldaeans press this passage above all, holding that by the northern one the Assyrians are meant, who had come from the north. Jerome: He inserted the north, so that we should understand not the real locust, which usually comes from the south, but under the figure of the locust the Assyrians and Chaldaeans. Abarbanel understands not only the Assyrians, who carried off the ten tribes, and the Babylonians, by whom the first temple was destroyed, but also the Romans, who destroyed the second. For all of these live to the north of Judaea, yet in such a way that the Assyrians and Babylonians lie toward the east and the Romans toward the west. And accordingly he holds that the Prophet placed some of these northerners at the face and others at the rear, since for the Hebrews the east is regarded as the face of the world and the west as its hinder part. But it is plain that this too pertains to the locusts by which Judaea was to be laid waste. With respect, namely, to Jerusalem, the city in which Joel seems to have prophesied, these locusts were either to the north, or to the east, or to the west. He does not mention southern ones because, since Jerusalem lay almost at the far south of the land of Canaan, the southern ones were few in relation to the city and were included under the others. With this premised, [III, 317] the words of the Prophet will contain nothing to detain the reader. The northern one, he says (that is, the part of the army of locusts which is to the north of the city), I will remove far from you, and drive it into a dry and desolate land, that is, into the deserts of Arabia. Its face toward the eastern sea, that is, [col. 481] the part turned toward the face of the world (or toward the east), into the Dead Sea, situated to the east of the city; and its rear toward the hinder sea, that is, the western part of the army into the western, or Mediterranean, sea. And its stench shall go up, its foulness (I say) shall go up. Its stench and its foulness are in Hebrew באשו and צחנהו; of these the latter occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew text, but is used by the Chaldee paraphrast at Ezech. XXIII, 20. For the Syrians too ܨܚܢܐ is the very same thing, with the guttural elided. Why then do the Greek translators here have Ἀναβήσεται ὁ βρόμος αὐτοῦ [Anabēsetai ho bromos autou], His noise shall go up? Hence Cyril: Ἐκεῖ τὸν βροῦχον καὶ τὴν ἀκρίδα διολέσαι φησι, δυσαχθῆ δὲ γενέσθαι τὸν βρόμον αὐτῶν [Ekei ton brouchon kai tēn akrida diolesai phēsi, dysachthē de genesthai ton bromon autōn]; There (in the Mediterranean sea) he says the bruchus and the locust perished, but their noise was grievous. I say that in both places there is a corruption, and that instead of βρόμον [bromon] one should read βρῶμον [brōmon], as Theodoret quite rightly has ^{(5)}. For βρῶμος [brōmos] is stench, whence βρωμώδης [brōmōdēs], for fetid and rank, occurs frequently in Dioscorides and Athenaeus. But nothing is more frequent than this corruption. So also in Hesychius βρόμος [bromos] is rendered ὀσμὴ [osmē]. And in Dioscorides, book 5, sea water kept for a long time at length becomes ἄβρομος [abromos], that is, loses its rankness. And in Athenaeus, book 3, chapter 33: Τάριχος τέλειος, καὶ μὴ βρομώδης [Tarichos teleios, kai mē bromōdēs]; Salted fish perfectly cured, and not rank. That this is the very same as the Hebrew צחנה you may gather also from the fact that the Talmudists call small salted fish צחנתא, and the Arabs صحناة [ṣaḥnāh], namely from their rank smell. This, then, is what Joel says: that the locusts, plunged into the sea, would give off a foul and rank odour. Moreover, that they are often carried off by the wind from the lands they devastate and plunged into the seas, we have shown ^{f)} from Pliny, Jerome and Orosius, on the words of Moses Exod. X, 19: God sent a west wind which, bringing the locusts, cast them into the Red Sea. As to what is added about the foul odour, it is proved by these words of Jerome about the locusts whose swarms, he writes, covered Judaea in his own time: When the wind rose, they were cast headlong into the first and the last sea, etc. And when the shores of both seas were filled with heaps of dead locusts which the waters had vomited up, [III, 318] their putrefaction and stench were so noxious that it even corrupted the air, and a pestilence arose among beasts as well as men. And so too what Augustine ^{g)}, Orosius ^{h)}, Freculphus ^{i)}, etc. relate, after Julius Obsequens and other older writers: that in the consulship of M. Plautius and M. Fulvius Flaccus, when the winds had cast an immense multitude of locusts into the African sea and the waves had driven them onto the shores, their wasting and putrefied mass gave off so pestilential a vapour that in Numidia alone eight hundred thousand people are reported to have perished, and on the coast around Carthage and Utica more than two hundred thousand; and at Utica itself thirty thousand soldiers, who had been stationed there to garrison all Africa, were destroyed and wiped out. Sigebert too, in the place cited above, relates that a multitude of locusts which had devastated Gaul, carried off by the blast of the winds and drowned in the British sea, was thrown back onto the shore by the backwash of the Ocean, and from its stench produced a corruption of the air, from which arose a great famine and a pestilence that carried off a third of mankind. More of this kind could be adduced, were these not more than sufficient ^{(6)}.
